elements.quote: The following systematic review explores the uses and understandings of physical, human-to-human touch engagements in healthcare professions.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: this review sought to understand the communicative, social and affective dimensions of touches a part of healthcare, medical or nursing interventions
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective of the review explicitly.

elements.quote: The synthesis produced was informed by 36 empirical studies involving either direct observation of touch practices, or recollection and discussion with healthcare professionals.
elements.reason: The abstract does not specify inclusion/exclusion criteria; it only implies empirical studies were included without stating eligibility criteria.

elements.quote: The studies were selected from five databases in March 2022.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the search date but does not name the databases or other information sources.

elements.quote: underwent quality appraisal through the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the MMAT was used for quality appraisal/risk of bias assessment.

elements.quote: The final dataset was then analysed, synthesised and presented according to the principles of thematic synthesis.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the synthesis method (thematic synthesis).

elements.quote: The synthesis produced was informed by 36 empirical studies involving either direct observation of touch practices, or recollection and discussion with healthcare professionals.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included studies (36) and brief study types, but does not report the number of participants or detailed study characteristics.

elements.quote: We outline how medical touch has been mostly categorised as either 'instrumental' or 'expressive', with only the latter usually described as serving a communicative purpose, despite its lower incidence.
elements.reason: The abstract presents the main (narrative/thematic) results of the synthesis.

elements.quote: Thematic synthesis was preferred over meta-aggregation for two main reasons.
elements.reason: No meta-analysis was conducted; the review used thematic synthesis, so no summary estimate applies.

elements.quote: the aim of this review was that of opening new pathways for the study of touch, rather than providing guidelines for practitioners
elements.reason: No group comparisons with effect directions were performed in this thematic synthesis.

elements.quote: Limitations The review could be at risk of bias given it sampled only studies written in English, French, Italian, Spanish and Finnish, thus not highlighting potentially different cultural and theoretical perspectives emerging from nonEuroAmerican contexts.
elements.reason: The abstract section includes a Limitations paragraph summarizing limitations of the evidence.

elements.quote: We argue that communication might happen in all instances of touch, while also advocating for empirical work to outline and describe the adaptive physical dynamics
elements.reason: The Conclusion section of the abstract provides a general interpretation and implications for future research.
No funding statement is present in the retrieved abstract content; only the internal checklist table claims item 11 was reported, without abstract text evidence.

elements.quote: Systematic review registration This review was not registered.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states the review was not registered, which satisfies reporting of registration status (consistent with the checklist marking item 12 as NO).

elements.quote: In light of this brief background analysis, the present review sets itself apart from previous ones by attempting to understand the communicative, social and affective dimensions of touch in healthcare and nursing professions... teases out conceptual and methodological issues that might have been partly obscured in the studies examined and overlooked in previous reviews.
elements.reason: The Aim section describes the current state of knowledge (previous reviews providing descriptive accounts, obscured conceptual/methodological issues) and the uncertainties the review addresses; the Abstract background also frames existing understanding of touch as instrumental vs expressive.

elements.quote: the present review sets itself apart from previous ones by attempting to understand the communicative, social and affective dimensions of touch in healthcare and nursing professions, in both its instrumental and expressive instances.
elements.reason: The importance and need for the review are explained: prior reviews gave descriptive accounts and overlooked socio-affective dimensions, motivating a new critical synthesis (supported also by text_9: 'most of the reviews on the topic generated thus far have focused on providing descriptive accounts').

elements.quote: First, most of the reviews on the topic generated thus far have focused on providing descriptive accounts to guide practitioners and policymakers.
elements.reason: The need for the current review relative to existing reviews is explained (previous reviews were descriptive; this one is critical/theoretical), but the retrieved evidence does not show specific identification and citation of the previous review(s) as an update or replication.
This is a qualitative thematic synthesis of social/communicative dimensions of touch, not a review of intervention effects, so describing a mechanism of action of an intervention does not apply.
The review is an exploratory qualitative thematic synthesis, not an evaluation of a complex intervention with components and outcomes, so a logic model is not required.

elements.quote: A PICo (Population, Interest, Context) framework ([45]; see also: [46]) was used to formulate the preliminary question 'What are care-givers' (i.e. allied health professionals, nurses, doctors, carers) [Population] actual uses and experiences of touch [Interest] when providing real and direct medical care to patients [Context]?'
elements.reason: The review's objective is explicitly stated as a research question formulated using the PICo framework, and the abstract (text_2) also states the review's aims.

elements.quote: From this question, PICo was also used to devise inclusion and exclusion criteria and to inform an initial set of search terms.
elements.reason: The review is exploratory/qualitative rather than a review of intervention effects; the planned focus is stated via PICo (Population, Interest, Context), an appropriate variant of PICO for this review type.

elements.quote: Both qualitative and quantitative studies were considered eligible, but non-empirical studies were not ('non-empirical' exclusion criterion). No specific sociometric variables (e.g. sex, age, socioeconomic status of participants) were sought, and studies were not excluded on the basis of their design (e.g. number of participants, methods).
elements.reason: Study characteristics for eligibility are specified via the PICo framework (Population, Interest, Context), eligible designs (qualitative and quantitative empirical studies), and settings (allied health professions, nursing, medicine, care work), with detailed exclusion criteria in Table 1.

elements.quote: studies from all years and in any language spoken by the team (i.e. English, Italian, French, Spanish, Finnish) were included ('Language' exclusion criterion). Both qualitative and quantitative studies were considered eligible, but non-empirical studies were not
elements.reason: Report characteristics are specified: all publication years included, language restrictions (English, Italian, French, Spanish, Finnish), and publication status (empirical studies only, excluding non-empirical pieces).
This is a thematic synthesis of touch practices, not an outcome-based review; no outcome measurement vs outcome reporting distinction is relevant to the eligibility criteria reported.

elements.quote: themes were constructed inductively, with new codes and themes created as necessary. Furthermore, the review followed the principles of thematic synthesis [63], identifying patterns and themes
elements.reason: The synthesis approach (inductive thematic synthesis with descriptive and analytical themes) is described, but the evidence does not explicitly specify predefined groups used in each synthesis linked to comparisons in the review objectives; grouping emerged inductively rather than being specified a priori.

elements.quote: Two of them ('language' and 'non-empirical') were based on the team expertise and the general aim of this review (i.e. capturing empirical social analysis over anecdotal case studies or philosophical discussions)
elements.reason: Rationales for notable restrictions (language and non-empirical criteria) are explicitly provided, and Table 1 gives reasons for each exclusion criterion (e.g. neo-natal interventions excluded due to different properties of touch with pre-verbal children).

elements.quote: The first author of this review ran a comprehensive search across five databases in March 2022: SSCI, MEDLINE, ACM, CINAHL and OTSeeker.
elements.reason: The search date (March 2022) is explicitly reported for all five databases searched.

elements.quote: ran a comprehensive search across five databases in March 2022: SSCI, MEDLINE, ACM, CINAHL and OTSeeker
elements.reason: Database names are reported, but no search interfaces/platforms or coverage dates are provided.

elements.reason: The types of individuals contacted (field experts) are described.

elements.quote: Lastly, three studies were identified and added to the corpus by screening references in previous reviews.
elements.reason: The type of reference lists examined (references in previous reviews) is specified.

elements.quote: Coding and data extraction was carried out by one reviewer (first author).

elements.reason: Group discussion with the research team is described for consolidating codes/themes, but no formal disagreement-resolution process for data extraction is reported (disagreement resolution is described only for screening/appraisal).

elements.quote: the first author extracted data without the use of software, aside from a standard word processor and spreadsheet editor.
elements.reason: There is no indication that data were extracted from figures; the review is a thematic synthesis of textual data, so software for extracting data from figures does not apply.

elements.quote: the data analysis stage was not bound by any deductive framework. Instead, themes were constructed inductively, with new codes and themes created as necessary.
elements.reason: No outcome domains for which data were sought are listed or defined; data extraction is described as inductive thematic synthesis without predefined outcomes. The ENTREQ checklist (table_8) marks item 10a as 'N/A', but no outcome list is provided in the Methods.

The manuscript does not state whether all results compatible with each outcome domain were sought; the ENTREQ checklist entry for item 10a is marked 'N/A' without explanation in the Methods text.

elements.quote: The data extraction, analysis and generation took a bottom-up approach: while the general direction of the review was established at the initial stage, the data analysis stage was not bound by any deductive framework.
elements.reason: This conditional element applies only when not all compatible results were sought; the manuscript never states that a subset of results was selected, and its inductive, exploratory qualitative approach suggests no predefined result-selection process was needed.
No changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance are reported in the retrieved evidence, so there is nothing to report with rationale.
No changes to processes for selecting results within outcome domains are reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: themes were constructed inductively, with new codes and themes created as necessary
elements.reason: The review is an exploratory qualitative thematic synthesis with no predefined or prioritised outcomes; no outcome is identified as most important for interpreting conclusions.

elements.quote: Table 2 Study characteristics | Research questions | ... | Methods | ... | Context | ... | Participants | ... | Year Country | ... | Authors |
elements.reason: Table 2 lists the study characteristics extracted (research questions, methods, context, participants, year, country, authors), and the ENTREQ checklist (table_8) maps item 10b to page 6. However, the variables are presented as table headings without explicit definitions, and other variables such as funding sources are not addressed.
No retrieved evidence describes any assumptions made about missing or unclear study information during data extraction.

No tool used to determine which data items to collect is cited. The PICo framework was used for search/inclusion criteria and MMAT for appraisal, but not for selecting data items; extraction is described as inductive without a deductive framework.

elements.quote: quality appraisal and risk of bias analysis through the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) [51, 52] (Appendix 6)
elements.reason: The tool is named but the domains, components, or items assessed by the MMAT are not described in the retrieved evidence; only a reference to Appendix 6 is given without content.

elements.quote: Papers were appraised by two reviewers for methodological robustness, and for their utility for the present review.
elements.reason: No overall risk-of-bias judgement or rules for deriving it are reported; appraisal appears tied to eligibility/utility rather than a defined overall RoB judgement.

elements.quote: Papers were appraised by two reviewers for methodological robustness... Consensus was required for a study to be considered eligible for review, so the two reviewers discussed disagreements to resolve them.
elements.reason: Two reviewers appraised papers and disagreements were resolved through discussion to reach consensus; independence is implied by the dual-reviewer consensus process.
No evidence of obtaining or confirming risk-of-bias information from study investigators; no such process is reported.
No automation tools were used for risk-of-bias assessment; extraction was done 'without the use of software, aside from a standard word processor and spreadsheet editor'.

elements.quote: the review followed the principles of thematic synthesis [63], identifying patterns and themes with the aim of uncovering underlying and often covert issues
elements.reason: The review used thematic synthesis of qualitative and mixed data; nowhere in the retrieved evidence is any effect measure (e.g. risk ratio, mean difference) specified for any outcome. No quantitative effect measures are reported in the methods or results.

elements.quote: themes were constructed inductively, with new codes and themes created as necessary
elements.reason: No effect sizes were computed or synthesized (thematic synthesis only), so no thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect size apply.

elements.quote: the data analysis stage was not bound by any deductive framework. Instead, themes were constructed inductively
elements.reason: Since no effect measures were used in synthesis, there was no re-expression of synthesized results using another effect measure.

elements.quote: Thematic synthesis was preferred over meta-aggregation for two main reasons.
elements.reason: The choice of effect measure cannot be justified because no effect measure was used; the synthesis method choice (thematic synthesis) is justified, but that is outside this item's scope.

elements.quote: At the full-text stage, papers underwent a quality appraisal and risk of bias analysis through the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) [51, 52] (Appendix 6); ... Papers were appraised by two reviewers for methodological robustness, and for their utility for the present review. Consensus was required for a study to be considered eligible for review, so the two reviewers discussed disagreements to resolve them. No papers were excluded because of methodological quality, but 50 additional studies were excluded on the grounds of the exclusion criteria used.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the processes used to decide study eligibility for the synthesis: application of exclusion criteria (PICo-derived, language, non-empirical), full-text screening with double-screening and consensus, MMAT appraisal for utility and robustness, and examples of excluded studies with reasons (text_8 and text_9). Since there is a single thematic synthesis, these processes cover the synthesis eligibility decisions.

elements.quote: Salient information was first annotated via a first read-through, with line-by-line coding of each study. These initial codes were discussed with the research team (3 members), with the aim of identifying a set of descriptive themes to guide the following read-throughs.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes how extracted data were coded and organised into descriptive and analytical themes for thematic synthesis, which constitutes data preparation for a qualitative synthesis. However, there is no explicit description of handling missing summary statistics or data conversions (e.g., transformations for presentation), so the reporting is incomplete.

elements.quote: Table 2 provides a summary of the characteristics of the included studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes Table 2 as summarizing study characteristics, and the ENTREQ checklist references tables (Table 1, Table 2, Appendix 4) used to present study characteristics, quotations, and synthesis output.

No graphical methods for displaying results of individual studies or syntheses are described in the Methods. The only figure referenced (Fig. 1) is the PRISMA flow diagram for study selection, not a results display.

Although Appendix 4 tables map studies to descriptive and analytical themes, no explicit statement of the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs is provided in the retrieved evidence.
No non-standard graphs are reported as being used to display results, so no rationale for such graphs is required.

elements.quote: the first author extracted data without the use of software, aside from a standard word processor and spreadsheet editor
elements.reason: No statistical/meta-analytic software applies; the review used thematic synthesis, not meta-analysis.

elements.quote: the review followed the principles of thematic synthesis [63]... Thematic synthesis was preferred over meta-aggregation for two main reasons.
elements.reason: The alternative synthesis method (thematic synthesis) is described and justified with explicit rationale.
No meta-analysis was performed; thematic synthesis was used instead.
No meta-analysis was performed.

elements.quote: a heterogeneity analysis of the reported results (Appendix 5). The causes of heterogeneity have been mostly explained via sub-group analysis or methodological evaluation.
elements.reason: A non-statistical heterogeneity analysis approach is described, but this is narrative rather than statistical heterogeneity quantification; still, the method is reported.
No random-effects meta-analysis was performed.
No random-effects meta-analysis was performed.
No random-effects meta-analysis was performed.
No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed.
No statistical synthesis involving multiple estimates per study was performed.

elements.quote: Thematic synthesis was preferred over meta-aggregation for two main reasons. First, most of the reviews on the topic generated thus far have focused on providing descriptive accounts... Second... our interest lays in uncovering, exploring and understanding underlying theoretical assumptions
elements.reason: Meta-analysis/meta-aggregation was judged inappropriate and reasons for the chosen alternative synthesis are explicitly reported.

elements.quote: a heterogeneity analysis of the reported results (Appendix 5). The causes of heterogeneity have been mostly explained via sub-group analysis or methodological evaluation.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that heterogeneity was explored via sub-group analysis and methodological evaluation, but the methods are described only briefly; no detailed procedure is given.

elements.quote: Touch and gender | Strong interaction between the gen- der of the toucher and the amount of touch provided and its percep- tion.
elements.reason: Factors (gender, age, experience, context) and their levels appear in the Appendix 5 heterogeneity tables, but these are results rather than pre-specified methods, and no expected direction of effect modification is reported in the methods.
No statement on whether heterogeneity analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both.
No methods for comparing subgroup effects (e.g. statistical tests of interaction) are reported; the review used narrative/thematic synthesis without such methods.

elements.quote: Such heterogeneity might be partly explained by con- text-Routasalo's research is carried out in Finland, where cultural understand- ings of touch might be different
elements.reason: Informal exploration of heterogeneity is evident in Appendix 5 (e.g. context, gender, age, experience as explanatory factors), but the methods section does not systematically describe these informal methods, factors, and levels.

The manuscript does not identify which heterogeneity analyses were not pre-specified; in fact text_9 states the analysis 'was not bound by any deductive framework' without addressing pre-specification of heterogeneity analyses.

No sensitivity analyses are described anywhere in the retrieved evidence. The review reports thematic synthesis, CERQual confidence assessment, and a heterogeneity analysis ('a heterogeneity analysis of the reported results (Appendix 5)'), but none of these constitute sensitivity analyses assessing robustness of the synthesised results, and no sensitivity analysis procedures are reported.
Since no sensitivity analyses are reported at all, there is no identification of any analysis as pre-specified or not pre-specified.

No methods for assessing risk of bias due to missing results (reporting biases) are described anywhere in the retrieved evidence. The review describes MMAT quality appraisal and CERQual confidence assessment, but neither addresses reporting bias due to missing results.
No existing reporting-bias assessment tool was used, so there are no domains/items or overall judgement process to report.
No reporting-bias tool was adapted; no evidence of any such adaptation exists.
No newly developed reporting-bias tool is described or referenced.

Although reviewer numbers and consensus procedures are reported for screening and MMAT appraisal ('Papers were appraised by two reviewers... Consensus was required'), no reporting-bias assessment was performed, so no reviewer independence or disagreement-resolution procedures for reporting-bias assessment are reported.
No processes for obtaining or confirming information from study investigators regarding missing results are described; no such process was undertaken.
No automation tools for reporting-bias assessment are described or used.
